37-the-serum-stack.angle: Layering is not a knowledge problem, it is a physics problem. The market sells serums as a menu to be ordered correctly; the actual constraint is molecular weight and water activity, and once you understand that, the menu dissolves into a rule you can apply to a product you have never held. The reader's assumption is that more layers are better and that the expert knows an order; the evidence says the order is nearly the whole of it and that the expert has no privileged knowledge beyond that.

40-summer-skin-routine.angle: Summer is a humidity argument, not a temperature argument. The reader's assumption is that summer skin needs a different, lighter set of products; the evidence says it needs the same chemistry in a different order of emphasis, because what changes is the water in the air and the sebum on the face, not the stratum corneum. Fewer steps, better ones.

41-blush-history.angle: Blush has carried the heaviest cultural freight per gram in the Western cosmetic cabinet, and almost all of that freight was deliberately loaded onto it. The reader's assumption is that blush is a young, frivolous category; the evidence says it is one of the oldest cosmetics on the table and that its history is a history of toxicity and regulation. The article should make the reader see a €12 cream pot as the end of a two-thousand-year chain.
headings: Antiquity — the lead and the wine
The Middle Ages — the loss and the recovery
The eighteenth century — the toxic bloom
The nineteenth century — the powder compact
The twentieth century — the cream blush

42-mascara-history.angle: The mascara wand is a twentieth-century invention; the cosmetic on the lash is two thousand years older. The reader's assumption is that mascara is a modern beauty product with a modern history; the evidence says the pigment on the eye is ancient and near-universal, and that only the delivery mechanism is new — and that the wand's arrival changed what mascara was allowed to be. The article should end by making the wand look like a much more recent invention than the eye it dresses.
headings: Antiquity — the kohl and the antimony
The Middle Ages — the loss and the Islamic recovery
The Victorian era — the at-home cosmetic

43-the-five-minute-face.angle: Five minutes is a budget, and the interesting question is what a competent editor would spend it on. The reader's assumption is that a five-minute face is a compromised face; the evidence says it is a decision, and that the same five minutes can produce a face that reads as deliberate or as careless depending entirely on which two steps get the time. The article should argue that the lip and the brow are the two that repay the seconds.
headings: Step five — the tinted lip balm

44-cream-versus-powder.angle: The cream-versus-powder argument is usually framed as a contest between two products. It is actually a contest between two lighting models — cream refracts, powder reflects — and the reader's assumption is that one format is better for a given skin type, when the real variable is the light in the room and the amount of time the face has to settle.

45-dispatches-foundation-drops.angle: Three months with the new serum-foundation drops, and the finding is that the format is genuinely new but the problems are the old ones. The reader's assumption is that a new format means new behaviour; the evidence says the drop simply moved the coverage later in the day, and the price of that move is that the drop now has to do the job of two products. A dispatch should be honest about what did not work.
headings: What the drop does not do

46-the-skin-scent.angle: A fragrance worn on skin behaves differently from the same fragrance sprayed into air, and almost nobody is told this. The reader's assumption is that a fragrance is a fragrance; the evidence says the substrate is half the formula, and that the difference between a scent that lasts eight hours and one that lasts forty minutes is usually the skin, not the bottle.
headings: Step four — the do not rub

47-vetiver-history.angle: Vetiver is the most structurally important material in modern perfumery and the least visible one: the root is invisible, and so is the root's role in making a fragrance smell like a place rather than like a list of notes. The reader's assumption is that vetiver is a green, woody, masculine note; the evidence says it is a fixative and a base, and that its history is the history of a commodity crop and its labour.
headings: The twentieth century — the modern perfumer

48-the-perfume-house-visit.angle: Grasse's advantage was never the roses; it was the technical school, the harvest labour, and the few families who kept compounding after the flower business collapsed. A reported visit should make the reader understand that a perfume is manufactured at the scale of agriculture, and that the most romantic part of it — the harvest — is the part the industry is trying to mechanise away.

49-summer-fragrance-six.angle: Six people who work in fragrance say what the summer scent is for, and the answers disagree productively — which is the point. The reader's assumption is that a summer fragrance is a light, citrus, daytime thing; the evidence says the professionals treat summer as a solvent problem, not a temperature problem, and that the cheapest-looking answer is often the wrong one.

50-the-nose-as-craft.angle: Perfumery is one of the last crafts where the master-to-apprentice ratio is still close to one, and the profession's argument with itself is whether that ratio is a virtue or an inefficiency. The reader's assumption is that 'the nose' is a marketing term for creative talent; the evidence says it is a certification, a training system, and a body of technical knowledge that would take six years to acquire and that the industry still declines to explain to the buyer.

51-bob-history.angle: The bob is a century old and has been re-invented every twenty years since, but it is usually re-invented as a style rather than as a structural decision about where the weight of the head sits. The reader's assumption is that a haircut is a trend; the evidence says the bob is one of a small number of shapes that answer a specific problem about the jaw and the neck, and that the pendulum between the blunt and the graduated bob is a pendulum between two different claims about what a face is for.

52-the-blonde-history.angle: The blonde has always been a manufactured colour pretending to be a natural one, and its history is a history of the substances used to fake it — most of which were dangerous, and several of which are still in the bottle. The reader's assumption is that blonde hair is a look; the evidence says it is a chemical process with a cost, and that the industry has been quietly improving the chemistry for two hundred years while the appearance stayed the same.

53-the-daily-hair-routine.angle: Most people use too many hair products and wash too often, and both errors come from the same place: the routine is organised around the shopping trip rather than around the scalp. The reader's assumption is that the daily hair routine is a matter of finding the right shampoo; the evidence says the wash frequency is the variable that governs everything else, and that most of the shelf is decoration.

54-hair-heat-history.angle: Hair heat is a century-long negotiation between a tool and a consumer who keeps getting burned. The reader's assumption is that heat damage is a modern problem created by modern flat irons; the evidence says the heated iron predates the flat iron by a century and that the industry's real innovation was not the temperature but the marketing of a controllable temperature.
headings: The nineteenth century — the first heated iron
1960s — the geometric cut, the iron-set style

55-dispatches-combs.angle: Six weeks with four implements — wooden comb, metal comb, boar-bristle brush, modern detangler — and the finding is that the difference between them matters less than the difference between how they are used. The reader's assumption is that the implement determines the result; the evidence says the tool matters far less than the pressure and the direction of travel, and that a good comb is a tool you can feel the difference of in the first stroke.

56-the-towel-history.angle: The towel is the object in the bathroom that gets replaced on a schedule and thought about not at all, and the reason is that it was the last household textile to be industrialised. The reader's assumption is that a towel is a towel; the evidence says the last fifty years of terry-cloth marketing have sold a category that was for most of its history a piece of linen kept for a lifetime, and that the physics of a good towel is a question about water and time.

57-the-scented-candle.angle: A candle is a combustion device that the fragrance industry has decided to sell as a mood, and the two are in tension. The reader's assumption is that the scented candle is a lifestyle object; the evidence says it is a small burner with a safety manual attached, and that the difference between a candle that throws and a candle that smells nice in the shop is a load percentage, a wick, and a wax.

58-building-the-vanity-shelf.angle: A shelf is not storage; it is a decision about what gets to be within arm's reach every morning. The reader's assumption is that a vanity shelf is a list of products; the evidence says the shelf should hold five things and that the third one matters more than the price of the first.

59-the-makeup-brush-history.angle: The brush is the one beauty tool that got materially better inside living memory, and it got better by substituting plastic for animal hair — which nobody argued about at the time. The reader's assumption is that a brush is a brush; the evidence says the fibre is the instrument, and that the last twenty years have quietly rewritten which material performs better without a single consumer being asked to weigh in.
headings: Antiquity — the finger and the sponge
The eighteenth century — the sable brush
The twentieth century — the synthetic brush

60-the-evening-ritual.angle: The evening ritual is usually sold as a repair sequence, and the reader's assumption is that the hour before bed is a treatment. The evidence says it is closer to a transition, and that the steps which make it work are the ones with no active ingredient in them at all.
